sentences.text: The name Dolichorhynchops translates to 'long-nosed face' in Greek, though it may also mean 'eye with long nose' due to the forward placement of its eyes on the snout.
This marine reptile possessed an elongated, slender snout containing many sockets for its teeth.
Although the animal had thin, sharp teeth, very few of these have survived in the fossil record.
The genus was first described by Samuel Wendell Williston in 1902, following the discovery of the holotype by the teenager George Fryer Sternberg around the turn of the century.
H.T. Martin prepared the specimen, which was then reconstructed under the supervision of Dr. Williston before being named.
George Sternberg later found a second, less complete specimen in 1926, while Marion Bonner discovered another example near Russell Springs in the early 1950s.

In 2005, the oldest known remains of D. osborni were found in the Fort Hays Chalk, and the original holotype has been exhibited at the University of Kansas Natural History Museum since its description.
The specimen found by Bonner is perhaps the most complete known of this species and measures just under 3 meters in length.
Dolichorhynchops belongs to the family Polycotylidae, the subfamily Polycotylinae, and the parent group Dolichorhynchia, and it is classified as a reptile.
The species D. herschelensis was described by Tamaki Sato in 2005, while a 2008 study classified T. bonneri as the valid species D. bonneri within the genus.
Dolichorhynchops lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous period, with a time range from the Turonian to the Maastrichtian, between 93.9 and 66 million years ago.

Remains from the lower zone of the chalk, dating from the Coniacian to Santonian ages, were reported, and D. tropicensis lived in the early Turonian stage of the early Late Cretaceous, approximately 93.5 to 91 million years ago.

D. herschelensis lived during the late Campanian to early Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous and was discovered in the Bearpaw Formation of Saskatchewan, Canada, a geological formation from the Late Cretaceous (late Campanian to Maastrichtian).
